On the diagnosis — AntiGravity is mostly right, with one correction

Bottleneck A (mounting BrainPage on click) is the real killer. This is 90% of your problem. The moment you click, the browser tries to do all of this in the same frame the animation is supposed to start: spin up a WebGL context, download + decode 4 PNGs, compile shaders, build thousands of particle objects. That's hundreds of milliseconds of frozen main thread — which is exactly the "takes too much time to load and then stutters" you're describing. Fix this one and most of the pain disappears.

Bottleneck B (clip-path) is real but the analysis slightly mis-frames it. Clip-path isn't expensive by itself. It's expensive because right now it's masking a layer that's live-rendering two canvases. The cost isn't the mask — it's repainting a running WebGL frame + a running physics canvas on every step of the mask. So B is really a symptom of A. If the thing inside the circle is static while the circle grows, clip-path becomes nearly free and you keep your exact Lando-style reveal. AntiGravity lands on this in its Option 1, which is the right call.

Bottleneck C (mix-blend screen at 150× scale) is real but minor. Worth a small tweak later, not the headline.

So the core principle to internalize: never animate a mask over a live, heavy layer. Freeze the layer, animate the mask, then bring the layer to life after. That single idea fixes the transition.

The bigger decision: click vs. auto-advance

Your instinct here is good and I'd weight your user feedback heavily — "people didn't realize it was a black box they had to click" is a textbook discoverability failure. A hero element that requires a hidden interaction to proceed is a dead end for a chunk of visitors. Adding "click to enter" text would work, but you're right that it feels like a patch bolted onto a design that didn't communicate itself.

Auto-advance solves it at the root and it makes the performance fix cleaner — because if the transition fires on a known timer instead of an unpredictable click, you know exactly when it's coming, so you can preload everything during the loop and arrive at the transition with zero work left to do.

Three ways to go:

Pure auto-advance — loop plays, then it transitions itself. Simplest, zero confusion. Downside: removes all agency, and your cursor-glow becomes pointless.

Auto-advance + click-to-skip (my recommendation) — it advances on its own after the loop, but an impatient or returning visitor can click to jump ahead. You get the cinematic intro for everyone and respect people who've seen it. This is what most high-end sites do.

Keep click, add a cue — the patch. I'd avoid it given your feedback.

Given your box is already more of a cinematic loop than an interactive toy (the portal got simplified to a soft glow), it wants to be an intro sequence, not a gate. Auto-advance fits its nature.

The unified fix (high level — not the step yet)

Putting the perf fix and the UX change together, the clean architecture becomes:

Box loop plays (auto). During this window, quietly preload + decode the brain-page textures and pre-mount a static placeholder of the brain page (flat background + static head image, no canvases).

After the loop / on click-skip, animate the clip-path circle growing from center to full screen — revealing the static placeholder from inside. Cheap, 60fps, exactly your Lando look.

On complete, swap to the real brain page. Because textures are already decoded, the live canvases boot with no hitch.

What I need you to decide before I write the step

Interaction model — pure auto-advance, or auto-advance + click-to-skip (my pick)?

Timing — advance after one full loop cycle (feels intentional), or a fixed ~2–3s? And should repeat visits skip/shorten the intro?

Reveal visual — confirm it's "expanding circle reveals the page from inside, origin at center" (Lando-style), not "circle covers the screen then page appears."

Cursor glow — keep it as a subtle touch during the short window, or drop it entirely?

Tell me your calls on those four. Once you confirm, I'll frame the fix as a proper step (WHY / DECISIONS / picture), label where it runs, and wait for your "start task."

Yes — I understand exactly, and you've found the real crux of the whole thing. Let me name it precisely, because once it's named the solution is obvious.

The problem, stated cleanly

A logo-shaped reveal needs a known, fixed shape to grow. Your loop gives you neither:

It's a video → the cross is baked pixels, not geometry. Code can't "read" the cross shape to turn it into a mask.

It's always moving → at any given millisecond the cross is in a different rotation/scale/pose. So "grow whatever shape is on screen right now" has no stable target. Click at frame 12 vs frame 40 = two totally different messy poses trying to become an aperture.

So the thing you're worried about is real: you can't cleanly grow "the current cross," because there is no single "current cross."

The resolution (and the thing to internalize)

You don't grow the momentary shape. You grow the canonical shape — and you only ever fire the reveal at the one moment the loop is sitting in that canonical pose.

This is exactly what Lando does. His logo doesn't open from a random mid-scramble pose — it settles into its clean, finished form first, then opens. The settle-then-open is the whole effect.

Apply that to you:

Your loop has a clean canonical cross — its rest/seam frame (the windmill at the start of each cycle, before the tunnel scaling kicks in).

Auto-advance makes this free: you control when the transition fires, so you fire it exactly at the loop seam — the canonical pose. No mismatch, ever.

Click also resolves to it: on click, you don't open from the messy current frame. You let the loop glide the short remaining distance to its next seam (~0.2–0.4s), then open from the canonical cross. So click and auto-advance converge on the identical shape.

Because the shape is always canonical at open-time, "the shape is always changing" stops mattering — you've removed the moment-to-moment shape from the equation entirely.

Then: that one canonical cross becomes a single fixed mask asset (an SVG path or transparent PNG). The brain page reveals through it; it scales up to fill the screen.
